1211.event_title: Thutmose IV sets up the Dream Stela at the Sphinx
1211.event: A granite stela set up in front of the Great Sphinx at Giza records that Prince Thutmose fell asleep in the Sphinx's shade and dreamed that the Sphinx, speaking as the sun god, promised him the throne if he would clear away the sand that buried it. After becoming king, Thutmose IV restored the Sphinx and erected the stela to record the dream. Scholars often read the inscription as royal propaganda supporting the legitimacy of his reign.
1211.explanation: The stela is one of the oldest surviving records of a dream treated as a message worth honouring with action and a monument.
1211.tie_back: The kural's heroine wonders what feast she could give to the dream that brought her a message, and Thutmose IV repaid his dream-messenger with a restoration and a monument.
1211._accuracy_note: Next-best: the gratitude to a message-bearing dream matches, but the message concerns kingship rather than an absent lover, and the dream story itself may be royal propaganda (the stela's existence is certain).

1212.event_title: Mary Shelley's waking dream gives her Frankenstein
1212.event: In June 1816 Mary Godwin, later Mary Shelley, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron and their companions were kept indoors by bleak weather near Lake Geneva, and Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Mary struggled to think of one until a waking dream showed her a pale student kneeling beside the figure he had put together and seeing it stir to life. That image grew into Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818.
1212.explanation: What she could not find by trying while awake came to her only in a dream-like state at night.
1212.tie_back: The kural's heroine pleads with her eyes to sleep so that a dream can give her what waking will not; Mary Shelley likewise found in a waking dream what days of effort had failed to give her.
1212._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared idea is needing a dream to reach what waking cannot, but there is no lover or plea for sleep in the documented event.

1213.event_title: Ono no Komachi's dream poems enter the Kokinshu
1213.event: Ono no Komachi was a ninth-century poet of the Heian court, and eighteen of her poems were included in the imperial anthology Kokinshu, compiled in 905. Several are dream poems: in one, having seen the man dear to her while she napped, she says she has begun to trust the things called dreams; in another she says that had she known it was a dream, she would never have woken.
1213.explanation: Komachi's poems are among the most famous in Japanese literature on meeting a lover only in dreams.
1213.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that though her husband shows no kindness while she is awake, seeing him in dreams keeps her alive, which is the very theme of Komachi's dream poems.
1213._accuracy_note: Very close: the event is the writing and anthologising of poems on this exact theme; little is documented about Komachi's actual life or lover.

1214.event_title: Otto Loewi's dream leads to the frog-heart experiment
1214.event: The pharmacologist Otto Loewi, professor at Graz, said that one night in 1921 he woke from a dream about an experiment, scribbled notes and in the morning could not read them. The next night the idea returned around 3 a.m. and he went straight to his laboratory. By transferring fluid from a frog heart slowed through its vagus nerve to a second heart, which then also slowed, he showed that nerves pass signals by chemicals, work for which he shared the 1936 Nobel Prize with Henry Dale.
1214.explanation: Loewi's own account credits a dream with bringing back an answer that his waking mind had lost.
1214.tie_back: The kural says love's joy comes in dreams because the dream goes out, finds the one who will not come in waking life, and brings him back; Loewi's dream likewise fetched what waking could not hold.
1214._accuracy_note: Next-best: the dream-as-retriever idea fits, but the subject is science, not love, and the dream story rests on Loewi's own later account.

1215.event_title: Kekulé describes the dream behind the benzene ring
1215.place: Berlin, Germany, recalling his time at Ghent, Belgium
1215.event: In 1865, while a professor at Ghent, August Kekulé published his proposal that the six carbon atoms of benzene form a ring. At a celebration in Berlin in 1890 marking the 25th anniversary of the theory, he told his audience that the idea had come to him while dozing by the fire, when he saw a snake seize its own tail. Most historians accept the account, though some suspect he was strengthening his claim to priority.
1215.explanation: A fleeting dream image, gone the moment he woke, became one of the foundations of organic chemistry.
1215.tie_back: The kural says that a dream meeting is sweet for exactly the moment it is seen, just as a waking one was; Kekulé's brief dream image mattered only in the moment of seeing it, and he had to seize it before it vanished.
1215._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural compares the passing sweetness of dream and waking meetings with a lover, and no documented event shows that; Kekulé illustrates only the brief, momentary value of a dream.

1216.event_title: Coleridge's Kubla Khan and the person from Porlock
1216.event: Samuel Taylor Coleridge said that several hundred lines of a poem came to him in a dream while he was under the influence of laudanum. On waking he began writing them down but, by his account, was interrupted by a person on business from Porlock, after which the rest of the vision was gone. The surviving 54-line fragment, Kubla Khan, was published in 1816, and some scholars think the interruption story was an excuse.
1216.explanation: The 'person from Porlock' has become a byword for the waking world breaking into, and ending, a precious vision.
1216.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that if there were no such thing as waking, the beloved who comes to her in dreams would never leave; Coleridge's lost poem is the classic case of waking chasing a dream away.
1216._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for waking as the enemy of the dream, though the dream was of a poem, not a lover, and the interruption rests on Coleridge's own disputed account.

1217.event_title: Goya publishes The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters
1217.event: In February 1799 Francisco Goya advertised Los Caprichos, a series of 80 aquatint etchings, in the Diario de Madrid. Plate 43, The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, shows an artist asleep at his drawing table while owls and bats close in and a lynx watches. Goya's caption explains that imagination abandoned by reason produces impossible monsters, but united with reason it is the mother of the arts.
1217.explanation: The print became one of the most famous images in Western art of sleep bringing torment instead of rest.
1217.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks why the cruel one who will not come while she is awake visits her dreams only to torment her; Goya's sleeper is likewise beset in sleep by what he cannot escape.
1217._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it captures tormenting dreams, but Goya's subject is reason and imagination, not an absent lover.

1218.event_title: Henri Rousseau paints The Dream for his long-lost Yadwigha
1218.event: Henri Rousseau's last painting, The Dream, was shown at the Salon des Indépendants in Paris in 1910, a few months before his death. It shows a woman reclining on a red sofa in a dense jungle among animals and a flute-playing snake charmer. Rousseau explained that the sleeping woman dreams she has been carried into the forest, and he attached a poem addressed to Yadwigha, a Polish woman he had loved many years before; the painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
1218.explanation: At the end of his life Rousseau placed a love from his past inside a dream, where she still lived for him.
1218.tie_back: The kural says the beloved rests on the shoulders in sleep and slips into the heart on waking, never truly absent; Rousseau kept his Yadwigha present in a dream picture decades after she was gone from his life.
1218._accuracy_note: Next-best: a former beloved living on in a dream image fits the spirit, but the painting shows the woman dreaming, not the painter, and little is documented about the relationship.

1219.event_title: Tchaikovsky and Nadezhda von Meck: a bond without meeting
1219.event: Nadezhda von Meck, the widow of a railway magnate, contacted Tchaikovsky in 1876 and from 1877 paid him an allowance of 6,000 rubles a year, which let him leave teaching at the Moscow Conservatory and compose full time. They exchanged more than 1,200 letters, but she insisted they never meet, and apart from two accidental encounters they never did. In 1890 she abruptly ended the allowance and the correspondence.
1219.explanation: For thirteen years an intense, trusting relationship existed entirely at a distance, without the two ever sitting together.
1219.tie_back: The kural's heroine says only those who never see their lovers in dreams blame them for not coming in waking life; von Meck sustained a deep bond with someone she chose never to meet, finding presence without meeting.
1219._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the relationship was not romantic in any documented sense and involved letters, not dreams; it shows only a bond sustained without meeting.

1220.event_title: Lady Jane Franklin refuses to give up on her husband
1220.place: London, England, and the Canadian Arctic
1220.event: Sir John Franklin's Arctic expedition, which sailed in 1845, was never heard from again. His wife Jane supported the searches from 1848, offered rewards and paid for ships of her own; after the government ended its searches, she bought and equipped the yacht Fox under Leopold McClintock. In 1859 the Fox expedition found a written record near Point Victory on King William Island confirming that the ships had been abandoned and Franklin had died.
1220.explanation: While official opinion gave the expedition up, Jane Franklin kept faith with her husband's memory and finally brought home the truth of his fate.
1220.tie_back: The kural's heroine says the townsfolk claim her husband has abandoned her, but they do not see him with her in her dreams; Jane Franklin likewise held to her own conviction about her husband while the authorities gave him up.
1220._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for private faith set against public opinion, though the issue was his survival and fate, not desertion, and dreams play no part.
